significance.justification: Verified true, the conclusion would be that representations are "near-invariant to preserving transforms and sensitive to violating transforms" and that the resulting "Conservation-Invariance Score" predictively couples internal geometry to each law's downstream physical-inconsistency rate. This is a form-(iii) law relating measurable quantities rather than merely an existence claim: it establishes a representational phenomenon and fixes expectations about graded violations and future errors, although it does not establish a causal mechanism for those errors; the practical importance of symmetry fidelity is supported by model-design reliance on exact equivariance in work such as Batzner et al.'s NequIP and Bronstein et al.'s Geometric Deep Learning framework. True and false are distinguishable, but the negative branch mainly rules out this proposed geometry and read-only predictor rather than conservation representations generally, especially because the hypothesis bundles heterogeneous laws. After substituting away the specific invariance geometry and CIS–error coupling, the broad topic alone would not earn this score, so the claim's measurable predictive relation places it above the topic-median concept-probing hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handle is the "Conservation-Invariance Score," a read-only diagnostic intended to "predict where the model produces physically inconsistent outputs"; used per model and law, it is ex ante because an auditor can screen reliability before accepting or shipping later outputs, though it forecasts aggregate law-level weakness rather than individual failures. After re-extraction on a new model, the asserted low-CIS/high-inconsistency relation predicts what should be found rather than supplying only a procedure for looking, so ordinary per-model recalibration does not erase the substantive conclusion. The hypothesis asserts scope across molecular, protein, and materials models and roughly ten conservation laws, handing the result to model auditors, selectors, and developers as well as interpretability researchers, but it does not claim a broadly transferable corrective intervention or design rule. Replacing the claim with the topic alone removes both CIS and its forward-looking error coupling, so the topic-substitution check does not support the score; the specific diagnostic, lead time, and relation-level transfer do.
